headline: CEO Declines Half-Billion Dollar Offer to Give Boat Company to Charity
meta_description: After 58 years building Grady-White Boats from near-bankruptcy to $100M+ revenue, Eddie Smith Jr. rejected major sale offers to establish a perpetual purpose t…
summary_short: A North Carolina boat company CEO turned down roughly half a billion dollars to convert his business into a permanent engine for charitable giving.
body:
Eddie Smith Jr. spent 58 years working 80-100 hour workweeks to rescue Grady-White Boats from near-bankruptcy and transform it into a nine-figure revenue generator. Then he turned down multiple offers worth approximately half a billion dollars. His reason: to preserve the company's culture and convert its profits into lasting philanthropy. Smith signed controlling shares to a purpose trust, structured so they can never be sold, with the trust operating the business according to his values—including employee profit sharing and robust education resources. All remaining profits flow to a 501(c)4 social welfare organization dedicated to charitable causes.

Smith's decision was inspired by entrepreneurs like Yvon Chouinard, who transformed Patagonia into a conservation powerhouse. "I just think that those of us that are fortunate enough to be in a position to help others—it's really a gift to me to be able to do what I do," Smith told Fortune Magazine. His conviction deepened after personal tragedy: the loss of his wife and son to ALS made the massive buyout offers feel hollow. Watching CEO peers sell their companies only to see them lose their way—stripped of culture and purpose—confirmed his path forward.

Smith's journey itself reflects uncommon resilience. Born to a father orphaned during the Great Depression, he grew up eating SPAM three times weekly near the poverty line. He lied about his age to land a paper route job, then became the first in his family to graduate from college at the University of North Carolina in 1965. Finding Grady-White in distress, he borrowed money to take over, then forsook golf—his favorite pastime—for over three decades to rebuild it. Today, the company generates over $100 million annually, now permanently dedicated to the causes Smith holds dear.

Turned down roughly $500 million in sale offers
Revenue now exceeds $100 million per year
First in family to graduate college (UNC, 1965)
Inspired by Patagonia founder Yvon Chouinard's model
